We describe two patients with this syndrome 
who had GAD antibodies in both CSF and serum. Partial relief of the symp- 
toms in these patients by corticosteroid therapy provides additional evidence 
of an autoimmune etiology of SPS and of the role of immunotherapy in its 
treatment.

PATIENT 2 
A 53-year-old black man was referred for evalu- 
ation of a 2?h-year history of progressive stiffness of 
the lower extremities. His initial symptom was in- 
voluntary upward curling of the toes of both feet. 
Stiffness subsequently developed in the remaining 
muscles of his legs. At the same time, he began to 
have chronic neck and low-back pain. One year be- 
fore admission, the patient also began to have pain- 
ful spasms of his legs superimposed on his stiffness, 
usually provoked by passive stretching. His wife 
noted that his spasms ceased and his stiffness re- 
solved somewhat during sleep. He began to require 
assistance arising from bed and walking. There was 
no history of diabetes, trauma, seizures, myoclo- 
nus, weakness, or sensory symptoms. The patient 
had been treated unsuccessfully with nonsteroidal 
antiinflammatory medications, sodium dantrolene, 
carbamazepine, trihexyphenidyl, and carbidopa/ 
levodopa (Sinemet). Treatment with phenytoin af- 
forded him mild relief. Low-dose diazepam moder- 
ately improved his stiffness and he was able to walk 
without assistance. One of the patient’s sisters has 
IDDM; otherwise, the family history was unre- 
markable.

General physical and neurological examination 
results were normal except for the motor system. 
Tone and strength were normal in the arms, but 
tone was markedly increased in all muscle groups of 
the legs, with dystonic posturing of both feet man- 
ifesting as extension of the metatarsal-phalangeal 
joints and flexion of the distal interphalangeal 
joints. Strength of the legs was difficult to assess 
because of rigidity. Deep tendon reflexes were nor- 
mal throughout and plantar reflexes were silent. 
The patient walked stiffly and turned with great dif- 
ficulty.

legs nearly normally. CSF glucose, protein, and cell 
count were unremarkable and there were no oligo- 
clonal bands. CSF IgG/albumin ratio was normal. 
Autoantibodies to GAD were detected in both se- 
rum and CSF by the method of Solimena et al. (4). 
In addition, gastric parietal cell, pancreatic islet 
cell, microsomal, and thyroglobulin autoantibodies 
were all present in the patient’s serum. This patient 
was reported as case 20 in the second report of 
Solimena et al. (5). The human lymphocyte antigen 
(HLA) phenotype of the patient was A3,24; 
B14(w6),w57(w4); DRw6,7(DQw1 ,w3; DRw52,53).

At the time of admission, diazepam therapy was 
withdrawn slowly to determine the baseline muscle 
stiffness of the patient. After a few days, he became 
markedly stiffer (videotape segment 1). The patient 
then began supplemental treatment with 100 mg of 
prednisone per day for 1 week and then 100 and 20 
mg on an alternate-day basis. Within 10 days of 
starting prednisone, the patient began to notice a 
marked decrease of his stiffness (videotape segment 
2). He was able to decrease the dose of diazepam 
from 40 to 20 mg per day. A year later, his dose of 
prednisone has been decreased to 40 mg every other 
day, but he still requires 20 mg of diazepam daily for 
residual stiffness.

DISCUSSION 
Our two patients demonstrate the typical findings 
of SPS as described by Moersch and Woltman (1). 
Both fulfill the diagnostic criteria of Gordon et al.
